newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Finnair, Braathens, Transwede flag more links.
newsitem.headline: Finnair, Braathens, Transwede flag more links.

text.p: Nordic airlines Finnair, Braathens SAFE and Transwede on Thursday flagged further possible links after signing an agreement to cooperate on frequent flier programmes and fares on various routes.
"This is a first step. I would not be surprised if there were more," Erik Braathen, president of Braathens SAFE, told a news conference.
Last week the airline unveiled plans to join forces as competition increases in the Nordic airline sector.

On Thursday it released details saying from May 1 all frequent flier members of Norway's Braathens SAFE and Swedish domestic airline Transwede would be able to use bonus points on Finland national carrier, Finnair's, international flights.
Additionally, members of Finnair's frequent flier programme could use points on all Braathens's and Transwede's routes.
The three airlines will also cooperate on fares so travellers get one price for a ticket even though there may be two or more segments with the different airlines in one trip.
"We will adjust the prices, but there won't be a significant cut," Braathen said.
The airlines will extend the use of the Nordic Air Pass, which also involves Danish Maersk Air and the Baltic Estonian Air and Lithuanian Airlines.
Furthermore, Braathens Safe will handle Finnair's arrivals and departures at Fornebu airport in Oslo.
Analysts see the grouping of the three airlines as a move to close ranks against main rival Scandinavian Airlines (SAS).
The three have already been chipping away at market share on what local analysts call the golden triangle, the profitable routes between Stockholm, Copenhagen and Oslo.
Braathens SAFE last November launched regular flights between Oslo and Stockholm.
Maersk Air is to launch regular flights between Copenhagen and Stockholm, which will share codes and have joint airport handling with Finnair while offering cheaper fares than SAS.
Braathen denied, however, reports that his airline had changed its ownership in Transwede, in which it currently owns 50 percent with an option to buy the remaining 50 percent.
"We aim to own 100 percent in Transwede, so we might use the option of 50 percent, but we have not acted yet," he said.
Recently SAS announced plans to cut travel agents' commissions to five percent from eight percent for domestic flights and from nine percent for intra-Scandinavia flights.
The three said they were not ready to act yet, preferring to see how SAS fares by cutting fees.
"We will wait and see what will happen," Finnair spokesman Erik Bennedich told Reuters. "Then we might have to follow the general development to keep up with competitors."
